title: A fast day
hook: Wednesday or Friday, a small fast
tomorrow: why does a table for two take more work than a table for one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a small group: a few strands twisted into one cord. Your line was two or three. Today, a quieter practice for the middle of the week.

Wednesday, mid-morning. Someone at the next desk passes on the pastry and drinks water instead. No speech about it, no sigh, no post. If you didn't know, you'd never guess it was a fast day. So why skip lunch on purpose, and then hide it? According to Jesus, the hiding is exactly the point, and it starts with a strange instruction about washing your face.
screen: `SHE PASSES ON THE PASTRY.` → `NO SPEECH, NO SIGH.` → `WHY HIDE IT?`

segments.voice: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus talks about fasting the way you'd talk about something ordinary. He says “when ye fast,” not if. Then he gives one instruction: don't make a show of it. In the King James Bible: “But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret.” The fast is real, but it's private, a conversation between a person and God, not a performance. Here's one to tell a friend: an old Christian teaching called the Didache already gives the habit a calendar. It tells its readers to fast on Wednesday and Friday. That weekly rhythm still shows up today, in different shapes. Orthodox Christians keep Wednesdays and Fridays as fast days. Catholics keep Friday as a day of penance, some by going without meat. Some Protestants choose a day of their own. A weekly fast can be small: one skipped meal, no meat, no sweets, no screens until evening. The going-without isn't the point by itself. The small hunger is a reminder, each time it shows up, to turn toward God. And when going without food isn't safe, because of health, medicine, pregnancy, or a long shift in the heat, a fast can be from something else entirely. Quiet, small, and once a week.
screen: `WHEN YE FAST, NOT IF.` · `WASH THY FACE: KEEP IT SECRET.` · `THE DIDACHE: WEDNESDAY, FRIDAY.` · `SMALL, SAFE, AND TURNED TO GOD.` · then, large: `A WEEKLY FAST.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or reach for one nearby, and take one slow sip, tasting plain water the way someone might on a fast day. Then choose your day this week, and what you'll go without, something small and safe. Let the next sip seal the choice, quietly, without telling anyone.
A fast day. One day a week of small going-without, kept quiet, with a hunger that points somewhere.
Your line: a weekly fast. Small enough to keep every week, quiet enough that nobody else needs to know. Day 1699, done.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: life; the hook answers yesterday's question; Grace weighs a Friday fast against a hot outdoor shift; practice: a slow sip of water).
Didache 8:1 is paraphrased (Wednesday and Friday). The lesson leaves out the Didache's contrast with 'the hypocrites' who fast on other days, to avoid making another group the foil. Confirm.

Present-day practice (Orthodox Wednesday and Friday fasts; Catholic Friday penance, some by abstaining from meat; some Protestants choosing a day) is stated without counts. Confirm wording, especially for Catholic Friday rules, which vary by country.
Safety: the lesson names health, medicine, pregnancy and heat as reasons a food fast may not be safe, and offers a non-food fast. Keep it.
Original: νηστεία (a fast); Matthew 6:16 uses the related verb. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
